title: As the Word comes to me, Lalo
hookLine: as the Lord's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo (Tilang M1, ang 722)
tomorrow: The one whose head He guards

cards: A town is sacked. Tradition says Guru Nanak was there, at Saidpur, when Babur's army came down from Kabul, and that he was taken captive for a time.
Early in the path, we met this town's carpenter, Bhai Lalo, whose plain bread Guru Nanak chose over a rich man's feast. Afterward, Guru Nanak sang about what he'd seen.
And he addressed the song not to a king, and not to the crowd, but to his friend, the carpenter.

teach.h: AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK.
teach.b: The shabad is in Raag Tilang, on ang 722. It opens, in effect: as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo. Then it describes the invasion with terrible clarity.

teach.h: A WEDDING PARTY OF SIN FROM KABUL.
teach.b: The invader came from Kabul like a wedding party of sin, demanding a bride by force. Modesty and righteousness hid themselves; falsehood strutted about as leader.
The religious officials of both communities, the qazis and the brahmins, were pushed aside. And the women, the hymn says, women of every community, suffered.
Songs of blood were being sung. Two things stand out. First, the courage.
Guru Nanak names an invader's violence plainly, while that power was rising over Punjab. He doesn't soften it or flatter it. Second, why he can.
The first line is the key: as the Word comes to me, so I speak. The word is baani, the same word that's in Gurbani, the Guru's word. Guru Nanak isn't offering his own opinion about politics.

He's saying the Word moves through him, and he won't edit it to keep himself safe. The line is often quoted as a standard for honest speech: say what is true, as it comes, even to power. And notice who hears it first.

teach.h: TOLD FIRST TO A WORKING FRIEND.
teach.b: Lalo, a working man, a friend who lived under that power.
The shabad can be heard as grief, as protest, and as a sign that the Word would not stay silent.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo, one of the hymns known as the Babar Vani, and cite its opening line as a model of fearless, truthful speech.

o: a song of grief sung after a battle
the Word, speech that comes from the Master

games.q: as the Word comes — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak softened his account to stay safe
he named the invasion's violence plainly, as the Word came.
the shabad is addressed to Bhai Lalo, a carpenter
the truth about power, told first to a working friend.
the hymn says only one community suffered
it says women of every community suffered, and officials of both were pushed aside.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, just after Saidpur is sacked by an invading army. what do you do?
o: sing what you saw, plainly, to your friend Lalo.
write a letter praising the new ruler.
games.why: as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo. he named the violence and would not edit the Word.

practice: Think of something true you've been holding back, at work, in your family, with a friend: not a cruel truth or a rant, but a true one, said with care.
Notice whether you've been editing it to keep yourself safe, and picture saying it plainly, as it comes, to the right person. If you pray, ask the One for courage with a quiet Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Baani, the Word, speech from the Master: Guru Nanak to Bhai Lalo, as it comes to me, so I speak, even about an invader's violence.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the Word, speech from the Master; khasam kee baanee, the Master's Word.

carryVoice: Your line: as the word comes. Plain speech doesn't have to be cruel. Six hundred fifty-nine days in.

sources.ref: Tilang M1, Ang 722–723 (jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee)
